16.59 Modal Analysis (POD, sPOD, mPOD & FMD)
Modal Analysis offer four different decompositions of data series
l Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (Classic POD)
l Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (sPOD)
l Multi-Scale Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (mPOD)
l Fourier Mode Decomposition (FMD)
Pleasenote:Thelastthreearedongleprotectedandmakessensefortime-resolvedinputonly!
Decompositionsnotsupportedbythedonglewillbevisibleintherecipebutgreyedoutsotheuser
cannotselectthem.
IfdatafromasPOD,mPODorFMDanalysisisavailablebutthecurrentdongledoesnotsupportit,
PAGE|723
thedatacanbedisplayedandused,but'ShowRecipe'or'PerformAnalysisagain'willrevertback
toClassicPOD.
All four analyses decompose a 'signal' that varies in space and time into a series of 'modes', each
with a scalar amplitude λ, a spatial distribution ϕ(x)and a temporal evolution ψ(t).
Combining these modes the original signal can be reconstructed:
= Global amplitude of the n'th mode
= n'th Spatial mode, 'Topos'
= n'th Temporal mode, 'Chronos'
The square of the modal amplitudes describes modal 'energy' and modes are sorted by descending
amplitude/energy, so the dominant modes are listed first.
The Topos describes spatial variations and are independent of time.
The Chronos describe how each of the modes contribute to the reconstruction as a function of time.
These are independent of spatial locations.
By design the Chronos are mutually orthogonal so the dot product of a Chronos with itself is 1,
while the dot product of two different Chronos is 0:
For Classic POD the Topos are mutually orthogonal as well:
The modes may themselves provide insights into the data investigated and decompositions are
often used for reduced order modeling (ROM), since an excellent approximation to the original sig-
nal can be made from just a few of the first (high-energy) modes. The first modes typically describe
large scale coherent structures, while the last modes often describe only noise.
Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) was first introduced in the context of Fluid Mechanics by
Lumley in 1967 1 . It is closely related to Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Com-
ponent Analysis (PCA) from linear algebra. The original POD analysis will find spatial modes only,
but adding the temporal modes also is straightforward. For classic POD both spatial and temporal
modes are orthogonal, so Aubry et al 2called it Bi-Orthogonal Decomposition (BOD) and also
coined the names 'Topos' and 'Chronos' for spatial and temporal modes respectively. There are
many other names for the technique, but the popular 'POD' is used here, while the names 'Topos'
and 'Chronos' from Aubry et al are adopted.
Classic POD is energy optimal in the sense that each new mode added recovers as much as pos-
sible of the energy from the original data. But all POD Chronos are broadband in the frequency
domain and may include signal content all the way from DC to the Nyquist limit (half the sample rate
of the original data). Fourier Mode Decomposition (FMD), as described by e.g. Ma et al in 20151, is
1Ma, L., Feng, L., Pan, C. et al. (2015):
Fourier mode decomposition of PIV data.
Sci. China Technol. Sci. 58, 1935–1948, 19 August 2015.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11431-015-5908-y
PAGE|724
spectrally pure so each Chronos has one specific frequency, but it is not optimal in terms of modal
energy distribution. As a compromise between energy optimality and spectral purity Sieber et al pro-
posed Spectral POD (sPOD) in 2016 1 and Mendez et al proposed Multi-Scale POD (mPOD) in
20193,4.
Both sPOD, mPOD and FMD has been incorporated into DynamicStudio as possible alternatives to
Classic POD.
To perform a complete or partial reconstruction from an existing Modal Analysis, please see "Modal
Reconstruction / Projection" on page 757.
16.59.1 Supported input
Most of the following examples assume that u represent (2C) velocity vectors from a time series of
planar (2D) vector maps. But the input data can be any time series of vectors or scalars in a planar
or volumetric spatial domain, so it could also be e.g. Volumetric PIV (3D3C), Stereo-PIV (2D3C),
scalar maps (2D1C) or pixel values from an image. Scalar maps can represent any physical quant-
ity, while velocity vectors are the only multivariate input with a dedicated display.
Modal Analysis can handle time series with up to 16000 datasets.
The Topos will inherit the type of the parent data, so if input data are vector maps, Topos will be vec-
tor maps also, if Scalar Maps are provided as input the Topos will also become scalar maps and if
input is images, Topos will become images as well.
Amplitude, Chronos and other properties derived from those are the same no matter what kind of
input is used.
16.59.2 Recipe & settings
Select an input ensemble of images, scalar or vector maps and select analysis method 'Modal Ana-
lysis':

Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition
Journal of Fluid Mechanics, Volume 792, pp. 798-828, March 2016
PAGE|725
16.59.3 Modal Analysis recipe
Input data will start loading as soon as the recipe opens as shown by a progress bar at the bottom
of the recipe. The data in each dataset will be organized in a so-called 'Snapshot' vector and a
Covariance matrix is built up by computing the dot product between such snapshot vectors from the
different timesteps (datasets). The main diagonal of the Covariance matrix holds the dot product of
each snapshot vector with itself and right next to those are the dot product of temporal neighbors. N
datasets will create N snapshot vectors and a symmetric NxN Covariance matrix. While filling in the
Covariance matrix as many snapshots as possible are stored in RAM, but with many and/or large
datasets there may not be room for them all in which case some of the datasets will have to be
loaded from disk several times. For every N'th of the Covariance values filled in the progress bar is
updated and a preliminary 2D Fourier Transform computed from the present Covariance matrix
(with zeros for the values not yet filled in). From the complex FFT a real power spectrum is com-
puted and all energy mirrored into the 1st quadrant for display in the recipe as an image. Greyscale
values follow a logarithmic scale so negative values are common even if this is a power spectrum.
Recipe with default settings is shown below:
Frequencies on the horizontal and vertical axes are relative to the sample rate of the original data
with DC (0,0) in the lower left corner and the Nyquist limit in the top right at half the sample rate of
the original data.
Below the 2D frequency spectrum a 1D spectrum shows the values along the diagonal of the 2D
spectrum above. Frequency 0 (DC) is to the left and the Nyquist limit to the right. Color scale in the
2D spectrum and y-axis on the 1D spectrum are both logarithmic.
In the left hand side a list shows the parameters available in the parent datasets and the user can
choose which of them to decompose. For vector maps the default is (U,V,W), for other datatypes it
is the first available scalar. At least one parameter must remain selected at all times, if multiple para-
meters are selected, they must share a common unit. Beyond these simple rules it is the users own
responsibility if it makes sense to combine the parameters chosen. It is possible, but not recom-
mended to mix parameters that are mutually dependent. For example VorticityZ = dV/dX - dU/dY.
These three parameters are all available in the figure above and share a common unit, so it is pos-
sible to combine them into one analysis, but since they are mutually dependent, it will make little
sense to do so.
PAGE|726
Whenever a parameter in the list is selected or unselected, the computation of Covariance matrix
will start over and the progress bar at the bottom of the recipe jump back to the far left side.
Having decided which parameters to analyze the rest of the recipe is used to determine how the
chosen parameters are to be analyzed. Remaining recipe screendumps in this help file have been
cropped to focus on this part.
In the top left corner of the recipe choose whether to perform classic snapshot POD (the default),
Spectral sPOD, Multi-Scale mPOD or Fourier Mode FMD. Just below choose whether to include or
exclude the DC.
The differences between POD, mPOD, sPOD & FMD lie in what masking/weighting (if any) is
applied to the frequency domain Covariance matrix before it is transformed back to the temporal
domain for eigen-decomposition:
The sketches above illustrate the various weightings in the 1st quadrant of the frequency domain,
so DC is in the lower left corner and the Nyquist limit in the upper right. Weights are always sym-
metrical around the diagonal, which is always preserved and when applied the mask is mirrored to
the other three quadrants of the frequency domain. Both mPOD & FMD rely on frequency domain
masking, where all frequency components are multiplied with either one or zero. Spectral POD on
the other hand rely on frequency domain filtering, where all frequency components are multiplied
by a weight between one and zero.
Note that for FMD analysis it makes no difference if DC is included or excluded.
After frequency domain masking / filtering the Covariance matrix is transformed back to the tem-
poral domain and eigen-decomposition gives us the modal amplitudes (eigenvalues) and cor-
responding Chronos (eigenvectors). The Topos are subsequently computed by projecting the
original data onto the Chronos found.
16.59.4 Handling the Mean
In earlier versions of the POD Analysis the temporal mean was subtracted from the data before per-
forming the actual computation on just the fluctuating part. The mean was subsequently appended
to the results as 'Mode 0' with its own Amplitude, Topos and Chronos. This is now optional and, if
chosen, performed in the frequency domain. Unlike other frequency domain masking removal of
the DC (leftmost column & bottom row) is not shown graphically in the recipe. Within round-off error
excluding the DC via frequency domain masking gives the same results as before.
Including the mean makes sense especially when investigating non-stationary or transient phe-
nomena, otherwise excluding it is more in line with traditional Reynolds decomposition of a tur-
bulent flow into a stationary (DC) and a fluctuating part.
PAGE|727
16.59.5 Handling Outliers and Masked out data
While building up the Covariance matrix Modal Analysis will check the status codes of input data-
sets and accept both Valid and Substituted data. Masked out or Rejected data (i.e. known Outliers)
will however be excluded from the analysis. Masking is normally not a problem since a (Static)
mask will have accepted or rejected data from a specific location the same way for all datasets in
the parent ensemble, so each location will have either all valid data or no data at all. Dynamic Mask-
ing or Outliers that have been detected, but not substituted, does however present a problem since
data from these locations will be gappy, providing information for some, but not all of the timesteps
in the parent ensemble. Modal Analysis will attempt to handle the situation by averaging over the
number of valid data samples from each location, but due to the missing data it is likely to get fewer
modes than normal and an exact reconstruction of the parent datasets is no longer possible. For a
modest number of outliers in the parent ensemble reconstruction errors will however be small and a
reasonable approximation should still be possible.
To avoid this problem it is recommended to make sure that the input datasets contain no known out-
liers before applying the POD Analysis.
"Universal Outlier Detection" on page 936 can for example be used to substitute outliers with a reas-
onable estimate based on valid neighbors.
If unsubstituted outliers are found among the input data a warning will be shown in the notification
area in the lower left part of the recipe, saying that
'Input data contain outliers! '
This is a warning that an exact reconstruction will no longer be possible. Depending on the number
of outliers the effective number of modes may be reduced and the ones found may be more noisy
than otherwise. It is however possible to proceed with the analysis and in many cases Modal
Reconstruction will still create a reasonable approximation to the original data.
16.59.6 Time resolved Input
For classic POD it is not mandatory to have time resolved input, but without it the Chronos are of
little use. Spectral POD (sPOD), Multi-Scale POD (mPOD) and Fourier Mode Decomposition
(FMD) on the other hand makes no sense at all without time-resolved input and the frequency
domain filtering require that the time between samples is constant and positive. If they are not a
warning will appear in the notification area in the lower left part of the recipe:
'Time between snapshots not constant and positive! '
The warning will appear if the longest and shortest time between consecutive samples differ by
more than 5% of the average time between samples. This allows for small-scale timestamp jitter,
but catches larger errors.
It is possible to ignore the warning and proceed with the analysis, but for sPOD, mPOD and FMD
results may not be reliable since the assumption of fixed time between samples was violated.
16.59.7 Mode Count
Modal Analysis generates modes, that are stored as separate datasets in an ensemble. The num-
ber of modes will be reduced if the input data contain outliers, but will otherwise correspond to
either the number of datasets (snapshot count) in the parent ensemble or to the number of values
in each of those datasets (snapshot length), whichever of these numbers is the smallest. Imagine
for example an ensemble with 1000 vector maps, each with 40x30 2D vectors. The snapshot count
is of course 1000, while the snapshot length is 40x30x2=2400 (40x30 vectors, each with a U- and a
V-component). In this case modal analysis will create 1000 modes, corresponding to the 1000 snap-
shots in the parent ensemble. If the experiment is repeated with a longer time series and generate
5000 vector maps, still with 40x30 2D vectors in each, modal analysis will however not create 5000
modes, but just 40x30x2=2400.
PAGE|728
Most literature assume that the number of values in each dataset is (much) larger than the number
of datasets and this is by far the most common scenario.
In the opposite scenario a warning will appear in the notification are in the lower left part of the
recipe:
'Snapshot count exceed snapshot length! '
Analysis can proceed, but consider reprocessing the parent datasets to get more values in each
dataset. For vector maps the spacing between neighbor vectors could for example be reduced in
order to get more vectors in each vector map.
16.59.8 Multi-Scale POD (mPOD)
Choosíng Multi-Scale mPOD as Analysis Type in the upper left corner of the recipe the right hand
side of the recipe will be enabled allowing the frequency range from Zero to the Nyquist limit to be
divided into blocks:
In the example above the frequency range has been divided into 4 blocks with 3 cutoff frequencies
between the outer limits f*=0.0 and f*=0.5. All frequencies are relative to the sample rate of the par-
ent data so f*=0.5 corresponds to half the sample rate, i.e. the Nyquist limit. Sample rate is shown
along with sample count in the middle right side of the recipe for information. The vertical slider can
be used to browse frequencies or a desired value can be typed into the entry field at the top. Press-
ing the button 'Add Cutoff' will round the desired frequency to the nearest bin edge, add it to the list
of cutoff frequencies and show corresponding lines over the spectrum displays. To remove a cutoff
frequency select it in the list and click 'Clear Selected'. 'Clear All' will remove all but the outer limits
0.0 and 0.5 in order to start over. Performing an mPOD analysis with no cutoff frequencies is equi-
valent to performing a Classic POD analysis. It is not possible to edit cutoff frequencies already in
the list, only to remove old ones and add new.
Transition bandwidth / Tapering
So far the frequency domain masking has been described as 'brickwall' filters with sharp edges
jumping from a transmission of 0% to 100% and back again from one frequency bin to the next.
This may produce undesired ringing phenomena in the temporal domain, which can be reduced by
tapering the filter edges so the transition from 0% to 100% and back again is gradual over a number
PAGE|729
of frequency bins. This is controlled by the 'Transition bandwidth' in the lower right of the recipe.
The smallest nonzero transition bandwidth corresponds to 2 frequency bins and filter transmission
will then be 0%-25%-75%-100%. From there transition bandwidth can be increased in steps of 2 fre-
quency bins up to a maximum of 16 bins. To ensure that transmission will in fact reach 100% before
it starts going back down again, transition bandwidth is also limited to half the width of the smallest
of the frequency blocks chosen. Similarly any nonzero transition bandwidth will limit how close to
one another cutoff frequencies can be set. It is therefore recommended to leave the transmission
bandwidth at 0 (brick wall filters) until all cutoff frequencies have been set and then apply filter edge
tapering at the end.
Tapering is done exclusively in the passband of each filter in order to prevent overlap and thus
crosstalk between neighboring frequency bands.
No tapering is applied to edges adjacent to the DC, whether it is included or excluded.
16.59.9 Spectral POD (sPOD)
Choosing Spectral POD (sPOD) as Analysis Type will apply a filter on the frequency domain Covari-
ance matrix, preserving the diagonal, but assigning lower weights the further we move away from
the diagonal. The falloff is Gaussian and the user can specify the standard deviation Sigma* of that
Gaussian. Similar to the cutoff frequencies of mPOD shown above, the Sigma* is also specified as
relative to the sampling frequency of the parent data. It can be set from 0.001 to 10.0, the outermost
values being for all practical purposes FMD and POD respectively.
The filtering is visualized in the recipe and contour lines show where the filter applies weights of
0.99, 0.50 & 0.01 as shown in the figure above.
Please note that the sPOD filter is in fact applied along the frequency domain antidiagonal only, but
shown on the main diagonal here, since all 4 quadrants of the 2D frequency spectrum are mirrored
into the 1st quadrant anyway.

Choosing Fourier Mode Decomposition (FMD) as Analysis Type will simply mask out all but the
diagonal from the frequency domain Covariance matrix as illustrated in the recipe:
PAGE|730
Note that the DC handling has been grayed out since it makes no difference here; The DC is com-
pletely isolated just like all other frequencies.
16.59.11 Modal analysis
When 'OK' or 'Apply' is pressed the frequency domain representation of the Covariance matrix is
masked/filtered as illustrated in the recipe. After masking the Covariance matrix is transformed
back to the temporal domain and eigen-decomposition produces eigen-values and -vectors, which
in turn leads to Modal Amplitudes and Chronos. Corresponding Topos are finally determined by pro-
jection of the parent data onto the Chronos found.
Comparing results from Classic POD, Multi-Scale POD, Spectral POD & FMD the sample Topos
below show the same physical pattern:

In all cases the green curve is the Chronos and the red one the corresponding Spectrum. The x-

All spectra show a peak just above 70Hz, but the result from Classic POD is broadband including

frequency band the sPOD Chronos shows a smoother falloff in frequency content. FMD results

Signal content at higher or lower frequencies is accounted for by other modes.
As with FMD (Fourier Mode Decomposition) the price we pay for spectral purity is a slower con-
vergence when reconstructing data from the modes. POD has the fastest possible convergence,
FMD the slowest and sPOD and mPOD are somewhere in between. This can be visualized by look-
ing at the Residual Energy Distribution as a function of mode number as shown below:
PAGE|734
With a residual of 1% we have recovered 99% of the fluctuating energy. In the example above POD
needs 150 modes to achieve this, while FMD requires 260 of the 420 modes available. Multiscale
and Spectral POD are all somewhere in between.
16.59.12 Mode Normalization / Scaling
As explained above, Chronos and (for POD) also Topos are by default orthonormal, meaning that
not only are the individual modes normal to one another, they also have unit length.
For the Topos this means that by default the Root (of the) Sum (of the) Squares of all displacement
components from all vectors will equal one. Similarly the Root (of the) Sum (of the) Squares of all
Chronos values should also equal one. From a mathematical point of view this is a perfectly normal
approach and corresponds to the default Mode Normalization 'Root Sum Square' in the recipe
above.
This approach however means also that the magnitude of individual vectors in each Topos will
depend on the total number of vectors and similarly the Chronos-values will depend on the number
of timesteps (/snapshots) included in the analysis. This makes it difficult to compare results from dif-
ferent analyses, so Mode Normalization may be set to 'Root Mean Square' instead. This causes
both Topos and Chronos to be scaled up so the Root (of the) Mean (of the) Squares of all elements
equals one. In effect this means that the average Topos vector has a length of one no matter how
many vectors there are and similarly the Chronos values will have an average magnitude of one no
matter how many snapshots/timesteps were included in the analysis.
To make sure the fundamental decomposition remains valid, the modal amplitudes are scaled
down, when corresponding Topos and Chronos are scaled up. Examples are shown below.
Please Note: For velocity vectors the normalization apply to the raw pixel displacements, not to the
metric velocities derived from them and shown as default by the vectormap display. Similar con-
siderations apply to scalar maps such as vorticity, derived from vector maps. In the examples
below the vector map display has been set to show pixel displacements instead of metric velocities.
PAGE|735
Mode 0 will usually be the mean of the input datasets followed by the actual POD modes sorted by
descending amplitude/energy.
The default display of a POD mode is the Topos, inheriting the datatype of the parent datasets;
When input is a series of vector maps, all Topos will be vector maps also.
PAGE|736
The Topos above are identical apart from the normalization. The first figure shows RSS-Scaled
Topos, the second figure RMS-Scaled Topos. The two are topologically identical, but note the dif-
ferent numerical values in the colorbar at the bottom.

been set up to plot Chronos as a function of Time and should give a plot like this:
PAGE|740
The first figure shows the result when using the (default) 'Root Sum Square' normalization, while
the second is the same data, but using 'Root Mean Square' normalization instead. As for the Topos
the two are identical except for scale (note the values on the y-axes). For clarity the plots above are
zoomed in on the first ~50 Chronos values instead of showing the full set.
A frequency domain spectrum of the Chronos is also available:
Black curve is the Chronos, red curve the corresponding spectrum. X-axis show frequencies, which
make sense for the spectrum only. The spectrum fulfills Parseval's theorem, so the sum of the
squares of the spectrum correspond to the sum of the squares of the Chronos values. Apart from
that the actual spectrum values have neither units nor physical meaning, the spectrum aims only to
describe frequency content of the Chronos and identify dominant frequencies if any. The example
above is from a mPOD analysis and this spectrum shows a dominant peak just below 200Hz and
no signal content at all outside the range 125-250Hz.
The XY Display Setup can in principle plot any two parameters as functions of one another, it is the
users own responsibility if the resulting curves make any sense. Chronos is for example the only
parameter that makes sense as a function of time and Spectrum the only that makes sense as a
function of frequency. All other parameters can be shown as a function of the Mode Number. Mode
Amplitude distribution is one such plot:
PAGE|741
As before the first figure shows POD results when the default 'Root Sum Square' normalization is
used, while the second figure shows the same data when modes are normalized using 'Root Mean
Square'. As explained above switching from RSS- to RMS-Normalization will increase Topos- and
Chronos-values and decrease modal Amplitudes. This is clearly seen when comparing values on
PAGE|742
the y-axes of the two plots above. For clarity both plots are zoomed in on the first 40 modes instead
of showing the full set.
From the modal amplitude distribution various other mode descriptors can be derived:
l Decay Rate quantify how fast modal amplitudes decay. Noise mode amplitudes tend to level off
so decay rates become small.
l The Energy Fraction is proportional to the square of the Amplitude, but scaled so Sum(Energy
Fractions)=1.0.
l The Accumulated Energy is the sum of Energy Fractions up to and including the current mode.
l The Residual Energy equals 1.0 - Accumulated Energy and describes the amount of energy
NOT covered by modes 1..N.
Please note also that the sum of the squares of the modal amplitudes represents the total energy in
the input data and will be the same regardless of the type of modal analysis performed, POD,
mPOD, sPOD or FMD.
Each of the Chronos furthermore has a temporal Lag-1 Auto-Correlation, quantifying the degree of
similarity between temporal neighbors:
This somewhat unusual formula is in fact the intra-class correlation exploiting the knowledge that
both values in each pair come from one and the same distribution.
The Lag-1 Auto-Correlation of a Chronos quantifies the degree of similarity (coherence) between
consecutive Cronos-values. A pure DC-mode, where all Chronos-values are equal, has a Lag-1
AutoCorrelation of 1.0, while temporally well-resolved modes will produces AC1-values that are
"large", but smaller than one. If the Chronos evaluated is a pure, noise-free sine or cosine, the AC1-
value equals the cosine of the phase angle between consecutive samples. If for example there is 8
samples/cycle the phase angle between consecutive samples will be 360°/8=45° and the Lag1-
AutoCorrelation will become AC1=cos(45°)=0.71. At the Nyquist limit of 2 samples/cycle there will
be 360°/2=180° between consecutive samples and the Lag-1 Auto-Correlation will become AC1-
1=cos(180°)=-1. This is very unlikely in practice, but negative AC1-values are not unusual among
PAGE|743
the higher order modes. In a temporally well resolved experiment the first few modes should how-
ever produce AC1-values in the range 0.5-1.0.
High and low Lag-1 Auto-Correlations can for example originate from a set of Topos and Chronos
such as these:
PAGE|744
Top: Topos. Bottom: Chronos. Left: High AC1-values. Right: Low AC1-values.
The next parameter derived directly from the Chronos is the Kurtosis of each mode. The Kurtosis is
the 4th order standardized moment of the Chronos:
The Kurtosis can tell us if the Chronos-values have reasonably constant magnitude over time or if
they are mostly very small with a few large exceptions.
If Chronos is constant over time (as in the DC-Mode for example), Kurtosis will become 1.0.
If Chronos describe a clean, noise-free sine-wave, Kurtosis will become 1.5.
If Chronos describe white noise with Gaussian distribution, Kurtosis will be around 3.0.
Some textbooks subtract 3 from the formula above to get 'Excess Kurtosis'; -This will be zero for a
normal distribution, negative for distributions that are more 'Peaked' than the normal distribution
and positive for distributions that are more 'Flat'.
PAGE|745
Modes with Kurtosis-values significantly above 3 may be caused by and describe only (undetected)
outliers in the input data. Such modes should of course be excluded from further analysis and the
Kurtosis is intended as a tool to aid the user in identifying them. Please note however that being a
fourth order moment, Kurtosis is a statistical quantity that may depend heavily on the number of
samples (i.e. the number of input datasets). In the figure above it appears for example that Kur-
tosis-values in the range 2-4 are perfectly normal, so one may question whether the single Kur-
tosis-value exceeding 5 is 'Significantly' bigger than 3. If in doubt please take a look at the
corresponding Chronos and/or Topos to see whether it contains evenly distributed noise or a (few)
dominant outlier(s).
The last four mode descriptors are derived from the Chronos spectra, quantifying the 1-50-99 per-
centiles of spectral power and the 98% occupied bandwidth. Mirroring the spectrum and squaring
the amplitudes gives a single sided power spectrum and the 1-percentile is simply the frequency
below which 1% of the total power is located (or, more interestingly, the frequency above which
99% of the power is located). The 50-percentile is the spectral median: Half the signal energy is
below this frequency and half above it. Obviously the 99-percentile is the frequency below which
99% of the spectral energy is contained and the 98% occupied bandwidth is simply the distance
between the 1 & 99 percentiles. The spectral energy percentiles interpolate linearly over each fre-
quency bin so for FMD results, where all signal is in one distinct bin, the 1-50-99 percentiles approx-
imate left, center and right side of the frequency bin in question. The finite and nonzero bin width
means that for the frequency bin centered at f=0 the 1-percentile is negative and likewise a fre-
quency bin centered at the Nyquist limit will have a 99-percentile exceeding that limit. There will
always be a frequency bin centered at f=0, while a frequency bin centered at the Nyquist limit will
exist only if analysis is applied on an even number of snapshots. For an odd number of snapshots
the Nyquist limit will be at the edge of the last frequency bin.
PAGE|746
The plots above illustrate the 1-50-99 percentiles of the various Chronos Spectra from Classic
POD, Multi-Scale POD, Spectral POD and Fourier Mode Decomposition of the same data.
For each mode a vertical line from top to bottom goes through the 99 percentile (red), the 50 per-
centile (grey) and 1 percentile (blue). It also passes one of the green markers indicating the energy
fraction of the mode in question. Frequency percentiles refer to the left (linear) y axis, energy frac-
tions to the right (logarithmic) one.
For the POD results the red 99 percentile markers tend to be at the top and the blue 1 percentile
markers at the bottom, confirming that POD Chronos are broadband with respect to frequency con-
tent. For the mPOD results are clearly clustered in 5 (user defined) frequency bands. For the
sPOD red and blue markers are pulled towards the grey diagonal line and for FMD they are just
above and below the diagonal.
Using the spectral median frequencies as primary axis can give a sort of spectrum showing modal
amplitude as a function of median frequency (vertical axis is logarithmic):
PAGE|747
Apart from the very dominant DC there is clearly a peak between 70 & 75Hz. Please note that for
FMD data there will be two modes at each distinct frequency except the DC and the Nyquist limit
where there is at most one. This is because the approach with frequency domain masking gen-
erates two real modes as opposed to traditional Fourier analysis, which would have created one
complex mode for each frequency bin. The two real modes corresponds to real and imaginary parts
of the complex mode and represent 90° phase shifted versions of the same spatio-temporal struc-
ture.
Please note that even for FMD analysis the output modes remain sorted by descending amplitude.
That's why lines have been switched off in the plot above as they would just be cris-crossing back
and forth in a confusing manner.
16.59.14 Numerical display
Apart from graphical displays, the POD modes can of course be displayed numerically as well:
The first 16 columns are unique to the Modal dataset, describing Chronos as a function of Time,
Spectrum as a function of Frequency and Amplitudes, Decay Rates, Energies, Lag-1 Auto-Cor-
relations and Kurtosis plus power spectral percentiles and occupied bandwidth as a function of
Mode Number. The remaining columns describe the Topos in the same way normal image, scalar
or vector maps are displayed numerically.
Browsing through the modes one by one will show that apart from the Topos, Chronos and Spec-
trum-values are the only ones changing. The remaining parameters are an overview and shared by
all modes.
16.59.15 Input requirements
Modal Analysis can in principle be applied to any image, scalar or vectormap ensemble, but mean-
ingful Topos require input that is spatially well resolved. Similarly meaningful Chronos require input
PAGE|748
that is temporally well resolved. If the flow being measured contain frequencies above half the
sampling rate of the measuring system, aliasing is to be expected and will affect modal results also.

In the first two columns there is one row per timestep and in the next two one line per frequency bin.
The number of lines in these two are always the same, but there's no 1:1 correspondence between

columns provide an overview of key figures for each mode, primarily the modal amplitude and prop-

Spectrum. For these each line contain properties for one specific mode.
But there is no direct connection between the timestep/frequency, the modal info and the data
points that share a common row.
Think of the Numerical Display as separate tables shown side by side. Normally the number of
modes match the number of timesteps, while the number of datapoints will typically be higher, so
the first 16 columns will typically have some empty space below the last timestep/mode. In some
cases there may be fewer modes than timesteps in which case this becomes very clear:

ing point images, so the exported TIFF images will most likely appear very dark or truncated black-

the files are in fact OK and will display correctly if imported into e.g. MATLAB or other software that
support and recognize floating point TIFF images.
16.59.17 Troubleshooting, Tips & Tricks
Modal Analysis will try to load as much of the input data as possible into RAM. But for long time-
series of large datasets they may not fit and DynamicStudio will rely on disk-swapping to access all
of the necessary data. Analysis time will go up, but should complete eventually. This requires how-
ever that 'Virtual Memory' is enabled and allocated in Windows Settings.

16.60 Modal Filter
This analysis method is an autonomous filter that approximates each dataset in an ensemble as a
weighted sum of all the other datasets.
It resembles and is inspired by "Modal Reconstruction / Projection" on page 757, but requires no
user interaction, projecting each dataset onto a full set of modes computed from all the other data-
sets in the parent ensemble.
Modal Filter uses temporal neighbors like "Temporal Smoothing" on page 912 and spatial neigh-
bors like "Average Filter" on page 524, but it is global and includes all neighbors in both space and
time while excluding the parent dataset itself.
PAGE|753
The analysis method supports planar or volumetric scalar or vector maps and require an ensemble
with multiple datasets as input. Images and voxel volumes are not supported.
It is possible to apply Modal Filter on an ensemble with just 2 datasets, but it will not make sense to
do so.
To work well the Modal Filter require a certain degree of similarity between datasets in the parent
ensemble. This means that it generally works well for phase-locked or time-resolved data, but even
for data that is not it may perform well if the data series is long enough and the process under invest-
igation is stationary or cyclic.
If the input data is insufficient the Modal Filter outputs will generally be biased towards the temporal
mean of the parent ensemble.
Modal Filter is inspired by POD Projection (see "Modal Reconstruction / Projection" on page 757),
which in turn rely on POD Analysis (see "Modal Analysis (POD, sPOD, mPOD & FMD)" on
page 722).
A given snapshot vector (dataset) XA can be approximated by projection onto a set of Topos F

derived from similar data:
The Topos F

Resulting weights in Wdefine the weighted sum of datasets in XB that best approximates the par-

In Modal Filtering XA is the n'th dataset currently being processed and XB is all the other datasets in
the parent ensemble.
It turns out that both KBB and KBA can be extracted from the full Covariance matrix K=XTX, con-
taining the dot products between all datasets in the parent ensemble as illustrated below. Grayed
out rows & columns illustrate the effect of masking out the n'th dataset:
KBB is simply Kwith the n'th row and column masked out (Green area in the figure above) and KBA
is the n'th column of K(Yellow in the figure above).
PAGE|754
Modal Filtering starts by computing the full Covariance matrix Kand then process all the datasets
by masking out rows & columns one by one before computing the pseudo-inverse and multiplying
that onto the n'th column of Kto get weights. These are finally used to approximate each dataset as
a weighted sum of all the other datasets in the parent ensemble.
To apply Modal Filter simply initiate an analysis and pick Modal Filter in the Post-Processing and
Visualization group:

Output is stored as a child ensemble in the database.

Like other filters Modal Filter data tend to be smoother than its parent data:

vectors are magenta. The background colors show the magnitude of differences between the two.
The biggest deviations between parent and child data occur where parent vectors do not match
local flow patterns very well.

highlight the changes:

Modal Filter can be applied to ensembles of Planar or Volumetric Scalar or Vector maps.
Modal Filter applied on a series of 2D1C Scalar maps (Vorticity in this case):
Modal Filter applied on a series of 2D3C Stereo PIV data:
PAGE|757
Modal Filter applied on a series of 3D3C Volumetric Vector maps (Iso-Contours show vertical velo-
city):
Filtered data is generally smoother than the parent data.
Modal Filter reconstructs every output as a weighted sum of all the other input datasets. The more
similar neighbor datasets are the closer the approximation will get. If input is time resolved neigh-
boring datasets are generally similar and the ones immediately before and after the current one will
typically be weighted high when reconstructing a dataset. If input is not time resolved the output
can still be reliable provided the experiment is stationary or cyclic and ran long enough that similar
flow patterns can be found.
Based on principles from POD, Modal Filter looks for patterns in the parent ensemble and discards
things in the current dataset that does not fit those patterns.
Known outliers, rejected by a validation routine, will of course be excluded from the analysis, but
the resulting spatio-temporal gaps in the data will disturb Modal Filtering and give less reliable res-
ults. It is therefore strongly recommended to substitute outliers in the parent data prior to applying
the Modal Filter.
16.61 Modal Reconstruction / Projection
Modal Decomposition (see "Modal Analysis (POD, sPOD, mPOD & FMD)" on page 722) is often
used for reduced order modeling since an excellent approximation to the original datasets can be
made from just a few of the modes. As implied by the name Modal Reconstruction is an analysis
PAGE|758
method to Reconstruct the original data from previously computed modes. A complete recon-
struction can be made, but most often a partial reconstruction is done, which use a chosen subset
of the modes to create an approximation to the original data, typically discarding noise and/or irrel-
evant background.
For Classical POD the spatial modes, 'Topos', are mutually orthogonal and they can be used as a
basis to approximate any dataset with identical structure and content by projecting onto these
modes. This is what Modal Projection does.
The input given to the analysis method determine what it does:
If the Modal Analysis is the primary (and only) input Reconstruction will be performed.
If the Modal Analysis is a secondary input Projection will be performed.
Modal Reconstruction and Projection share a common recipe, since both rely on the user to choose
which of the modes to use in the analysis.
Please note: In the examples shown here Classic POD Analysis and subsequent Reconstruction or
Projection is done on Vector Maps, but all can be done on Images or Scalar Maps also in exactly
the same manner. Reconstruction can also be done based on mPOD or FMD modes, while Classic
POD is the only one for which Projection is supported, since it relies on orthogonality of Topos, the
spatial modes.
16.61.1 Modal Reconstruction
If Modal Analysis is the primary (and only) input Reconstruction will be performed:
(cid:223)
The math behind Modal Reconstruction is embedded in the expression that defines Modal Decom-
positions:
= Global amplitude of the n'th mode
= n'th Spatial mode, 'Topos'
= n'th Temporal mode, 'Chronos'
Modal Analysis finds a set of N 'Modes' with Amplitudes l , spatial Topos f and temporal Chronos y
from a given set of input 'snapshots' u( x,t).
Modal Reconstruction does the opposite, recombining the modes to reconstruct the original data
according to the formula above. A complete reconstruction is of little or no use, but a partial recon-
struction can be very useful as a sort of filter to include only dominant features from the data and
exclude e.g. noise. Which of the POD modes to include or exclude in the reconstruction is for the
user to decide. (See the recipe below).
PAGE|759
16.61.2 POD Projection
If a POD Analysis is a secondary input POD Projection will be performed to approximate the parent
dataset:
(cid:223)
Using the POD modes as a basis the parent dataset is projected onto each Topos using a simple
dot product:
-with i=1..M summing over all measured values in all positions covered (for vector maps for
example this means summing over all u- and v-velocities from all vectors in the vector map).
Resulting scalar value an represents the contribution from Topos y
n in the approximation of u. Sum-
ming up multiple such contributions uis approximated:
If the parent dataset is among the ones from which the POD Analysis was performed a complete
reconstruction will be made if all POD modes are included in the projection, but as for
POD Reconstruction the Projection is normally performed with a chosen subset of the modes.
POD Projection can process parent data that were not involved in the POD Analysis as long as they
are the same type (Image, Scalar or Vector map) and has the same grid size (width, height &
depth).
When working with images POD Projection will inherit bit depth (8-, 10- or 12-bit) from its parent,
whereas a POD Reconstruction will always generate floating point images regardless of ancestor
bit depth.
POD Projection will accept only Classic POD as input and refuse sPOD (Spectral POD), mPOD
(Multiscale POD) and FMD (Fourier Mode Decompostion).
This is because projection relies on the Topos being mutually orthogonal. Chronos, the temporal
modes, are orthogonal for all decompositions, but Topos, the spatial modes, are orthogonal for
Classic POD only.
16.61.3 Initiating Modal Reconstruction / Projection
Modal Reconstruction can be found among analysis steps for Pre- and Post-Processing
& Visualization:
PAGE|760
The main choice to make in POD Reconstruction/ Projection is which of the POD modes to include
and which to exclude in the reconstruction. The recipe offers two different ways of doing this;
'Energy Fraction' or 'Selected Modes':
The last one, 'Selected modes', is the simplest; Specify directly which modes to include in the recon-
struction. The syntax corresponds to the one used in a printer-dialog, specifying which pages from
a document to print. One can specify individual modes numerically separated by commas and/or
spaces. Alternatively specify a range of modes by putting a dash between the first and the last of
the mode numbers in the sequence. Or combine the two, so for example '1-4, 6-7' would recon-
struct using modes 1-4 and 6-7 (i.e. 1-7 except 5).
The other option, 'Energy Fraction' is semiautomatic, including all modes from 0 or 1 up to the
mode where the accumulated energy of the modes included reach or exceed the desired fraction of
total energy summed over all modes. The checkbox 'Include Dominant' determine whether or not to
include Mode 0 (the mean) in the energy based reconstruction.
Please note that energy based mode selection rely on the modal energy distribution and thus from
the ancestor data that went into the Modal Analysis originally. For Projection the 'Energy' of the par-
ent dataset plays no role, but that should be OK as long as the parent dataset originate from an
experiment that is 'similar' to the one from which the POD Modes were derived. If it does not POD
Reconstruction makes little sense anyway, but DynamicStudio has no way of knowing, so it is the
user's own responsibility to choose suitable POD Modes when using POD Projection.
PAGE|761
Note also that a partial reconstruction of data will only resemble the original data on average. Most
often the deviations will be small and distributed evenly in space and time, but for data that is some-
how atypical much larger deviations may occasionally be found in isolated locations and/or
timesteps. If for example output from a temporal smoothing was used as input to the modal ana-
lysis all of the central datasets were smoothed, while at the beginning and end of the time series
there will be a number of datasets that have in fact not been smoothed and are therefore not similar
to the rest. Making a partial reconstruction from this will be fine for all the smoothed data in the
middle, but the first and last few datasets may not resemble their ancestors very well.
Note also that output from a Modal Reconstruction or Projection will always have dataset indices 1,
2, 3, 4 and so on regardless if the ancestor data did not start at index 1 and/or did not increment
indices in steps of 1. This is normally not a problem unless it is attempted to e.g. subtract two vector
map ensembles with mismatching indices from one another.
For projection the recipe will include a checkbox labeled 'Complementary Output'. When checked
the reconstructed data will not be returned, but instead subtracted from the parent dataset and the
remainder returned. This can be useful for e.g. background removal; If a subset of modes have
been identified as describing some sort of undesired background variations they can be removed
from the data.
The figure below shows a POD mode energy distribution from POD Analysis, both for individual
modes (blue) and accumulated (red). In this example modes 1 & 2 are comparable and combine to
cover more than 70% of the total energy. Modes 3 & 4 are weaker, but still relevant and including
these the accumulated energy exceed 90%. Energy based reconstruction with the default 90%
energy fraction would thus include up to mode 4 in this case. The blue curve hints at something rel-
evant from mode 5 & 6 even if they contribute very little, but modes 7 and up probably has little rel-
evance. (The first 25 of 249 modes are shown below).
Figures below show an example of Parent data and corresponding POD Reconstruction with the
default target energy fraction of 90% (i.e. modes 0-4 in this case):
PAGE|762
The Reconstruction resembles the Parent vector map so much there is barely any difference. Vor-
ticity is shown as a scalar map behind the vectors to visualize that the two vector maps are not
identical; The reconstruction is a bit smoother than the parent.
Reconstructing or Projecting from/onto specific modes is another option. Including only Mode 0 is a
(complicated) way of getting the temporal mean. Neighboring modes of similar energy will often rep-
resent 90° phase shifted versions of the same traveling vortices, so in the example above modes 1
& 2 are candidates for this as is mode 3-4 and even 5-6:

16.62 Moving Average Validation
This method is used to validate vector maps by comparing each vector with the average of other
vectors in a defined neighborhood. Vectors that deviate too much from their neighbors can be
replaced by the average of the neighbors as a reasonable estimate of true velocities.
16.62.1 Using the <Moving-average validation > method
To use this method the ensemble containing vector maps of interest and look for the method in the
category 'PIV Signal'. Parameters such as:
l The averaging area size (MxN)
l The acceptance factor (Ap)
l The number of iterations (n)
l
(and addition al options as well)
are set by the user. (Press the 'Default' button to get values of reference.)
PAGE|764
Note that the size of the (M x N) averaging area has no maximum and that M and N can be set inde-
pendently. However, the larger this area, the smoother the vector field becomes which leads to a
loss of resolution. (In most cases, M = N = 3, 5 or 7)
The acceptance factor 'Ap' is the single parameter used to determine whether a spurious vector is
found (inside the area M x N) and shall be replaced by a vector. This 'new' vector is calculated by
local interpolation using 'n' iterations. (Typical values are Ap = 0.12 - 0.15 and n = 2 or 3).
PAGE|765
(Top) Instant velocity vector map calculated by Adaptive correlation methodology (16 x 16, 25 %
overlapping) and (Bottom) moving-average vector results.
16.63 Multi Camera Calibration
The Multi Camera Calibration method is used to generate spatial camera calibrations, a.k.a. IMF's,
Imaging Model Fits, for each of the cameras in the system.
As implied by the name it is designed to calibrate multiple cameras at the same time, but they can
also be calibrated one by one.
It is based on multiple images of a calibration target with markers in known positions. The target
can be active, turning individual markers on and off in a controlled manner or it can be passive,
where all markers are illuminated at the same time. Targets can be chessboard or dot matrix style,
single-sided or double-sided and they can be planar or multilevel. Several known targets of varying
PAGE|766
types and sizes are in the target library or users can enter parameters of a custom target of their
own.
Often the target is traversed to cover a volume, but in some cases a pan/tilt approach can be used
with just one well-defined reference target position and orientation, followed by a series of images
where the target has been moved and/or tilted randomly to cover the intended measuring volume.
The Multi Camera Calibration method provides a fully automatic or alternatively a semi-automatic
calibration, which automatically detects individual markers but the user still has the possibility to
manually specify the origin of the calibration target. In addition, also a Manual Calibration is
provided that lets the user freely create a calibration grid with markers, to be manually placed on
top of the calibration images in order to relate the dimensions of the image to a coordinate system
in physical space.
The input requirements for the method is either single a calibration image ensemble or multiple cal-
ibration image ensembles from multiple cameras, which are then selected as fixed inputs. For
detailed information regarding acquisition of calibration images please See "Acquiring calibration
images".
One or multiple calibration image ensembles with acquired calibration images (with or without the
Z-coordinates specified) must be selected in the database tree. From the Calibration Tab in the rib-
bon select 'Calibrate...', or right mouse click on the images and select analyze, and in the resulting
dialog, select the method 'Multi Camera Calibration' from the 'Calibrations' group.
PAGE|767
The Multi Camera Calibration recipe is divided into four frames:
l Browse Datasets

l Calibration model
PAGE|768

refer to "Using the display from within an analysis method" on page 1017.

Normal Targets

'Target Info'.
If a Dantec provided target is used, this can be selected in the drop down list of known target types
will be enabled and you will have to specify the 'Marker Shape' as 'Crosses', 'Dots' or 'Check-
erboard'. Subsequently you will have to specify marker spacing and other 'Target Info' parameters
that depend on the target type chosen.
Apart from Standard targets the list also includes custom targets previously created and saved
(See Target Library & Custom Targets in Imaging model fit). In this case most target parameters
such as marker spacing will be locked to values loaded from the target library.
The only exception is 'Target Processing', that is relevant for checkerboard targets only; With dif-
ferent types of 'Edge Detector' you can choose between different methods for finding the check-
erboard crossings; The first 6, 'Detector_NxN', attempts to identify individual tiles on the
chessboard target and subsequently locate the corners of each tile. The last one, 'Detector_DOH',
compute the 'Determinant of Hessian' from gray-scale intensity gradients in order to identify and loc-
ate saddle points (=Crossings) in the calibration images. Generally the topmost methods in the list
are the fastest, that works best with high-quality images, while the last one is the slowest, but also
the most robust against e.g. blurry and/or poor contrast images.

When the Target Identification Type is set to Manual, the user is able to freely place the calibration

When Manual Calibration is chosen, first go to the Calibration Model tab. Here the desired Imaging
Model and the Coordinate System Orientation must be selected. For a detailed description about
the imaging models and coordinate system orientation please refer to Imaging model fit.

to overlay a default grid of calibration markers on the calibration image. Now, by going back to the
Target Info tab, the parameters of the grid and the markers can be changed. Adjust the parameters
so that the marker grid matches an object with well-known dimensions in the image.
Grid spacing:
Defines the physical distance in mm between the markers in the grid, in the x and y directions indi-
vidually.
Reference point:
Defines the coordinates (mm) for the grid reference point in physical space.
Grid size:
Defines the number of rows and columns of calibration markers used in the grid.
PAGE|772

PAGE|776
There are 4 groups of selections to make:
In the topmost group the user specifies whether or not previously invalidated and/or substituted
input data should be included in or excluded from the analysis.
In the second group the user identifies the temporal window from which the statistics should be
extracted. The default is 'Include All' and the recommended choice if the physical phenomenon
under investigation can be considered stationary at least for the duration of the experiment. If it is
not stationary you may choose to extract the statistics from a sliding temporal window centered
around each dataset. If used the temporal window length must be odd (to ensure symmetry) and
the lowest accepted (but not recommended) window length is 9, meaning current sample plus 4
before and 4 after. Please note that at the start and end of a dataseries (i.e an ensemble) the sliding
window is truncated since there are no data available before the first or after the last dataset. Con-
sequently the number of datasets included is even lower and with a nominal window length of 9 you
can have as few as 5 neighboring datasets included. Statistics derived from just 5 samples is obvi-
ously not very reliable and very likely to let outliers pass undetected.
The third group of recipe selections will show the various data available in the parent ensemble and
let the user choose which of them to include in the analysis. It is the users own responsibility to
make meaningful choices. In the example above you can f.ex. validate on the basis of pixel dis-
placements or measured velocities, but it will make little sense to include both in the same analysis
since the two are strongly correlated and including f.ex. U-velocity will provide no new information if
U-displacement is already included.
The last and final recipe setting is the limit for computed N-Sigma above which a sample will be con-
sidered an outlier. Provided you have enough data for reliable statistics reasonable limit values will
typically be 4-6, but please note that the number of samples included in the statistics limits the N-
PAGE|777
Sigma value you might find regardless of the presence of outliers. If you compute statistics on M
samples the computed N-Sigma value is limited to:
With M=25 samples you will f.ex. never get r-values above 4.8, so setting the acceptance limit to 5
or more is guaranteed to find no outliers at all no matter how bad they are.
16.65 Octave Link
The Octave Link can transfer data from the DynamicStudio database to Octave's workspace, and
data-analysis can be performed using Octave scripts supplied by the user. Results can be trans-
ferred back to the DynamicStudio database for safe keeping. For general information and doc-
umentation on Octave see https://www.gnu.org/software/octave/. Octave itself can also be
downloaded from there.
The implementation and integration of the Octave Link was by design made as close as possible to
the MATLAB Link. This means that most scripts developed for the MATLAB Link can usually also
be used with the Octave Link.
16.65.1 Contents

16.65.2 Installing Octave
Do not install Octave to the default path 'C:\Program files\GNU Octave\... '
Use another path such as 'C:\GNU_Octave\...' as the installation folder (simply remove 'Program
Files' and replace blanks with underscores).
For use on Windows the path may not contain blanks or spaces, whereas underscores are OK.
To transfer data between DynamicStudio and Octave a mex file called mmfile.mex is built. (The
source can be seen in mmfile.cc. The mmfile.cc will be copied to the bin folder of the Octave install-
ation when running DynamicStudio method "Octave link").
Building the mmfile.mex requires full access rights to the bin folder of the Octave installation. The
folder "C:\Program files" is typically protected by Windows and Read Only except with a admin-
istrator login. Access rights problems can be avoided by installing Octave somewhere else.

16.66 Oscillating Pattern Decomposition (OPD)
The Oscillating Pattern Decomposition (OPD) method is based on Principal Interaction
& Oscillation Patterns (PIPs & POPs) as introduced in 1988 by K. Hasselmann in the field of cli-
matology.
OPD is based on stability analysis of the mean flow and should be applied to time-resolved data
only. Any fluctuation of the flow is considered a kind of perturbation, which can either grow or decay
exponentially in time (if the flow is unstable or stable respectively).
The fluctuating part of the Navier-Stokes equation is modeled by a Langevin equation for a linear
Markov process:
,
where u(t) is a vector of velocity fluctuations, B is the deterministic feedback matrix and
is
noise driving the system (can be interpreted as the influence of smaller, unresolved scales).
The noise
forms a covariance matrix Q , while the process itself is characterized by the cov-
ariance matrix
:
.
The Langevin equation is a stochastic differential equation, which can be transformed into a Fok-
ker-Planck equation. It can be rewritten for lag time
as follows:
,
where G is the Green function, which in turn can be estimated from the lag- and lag-0 covariance
matrices::
of the feedback mat-
The eigenvalues gk of the Green function G are related to the eigenvalues
rix B as follows:
.
The real part of eigenvalues
characterizes the decay/e-fold time
of the k'th mode (should
be negative for a stable system), while the imaginary part of eigenvalues
gives the oscillation
frequency fk of the k'th mode:
.
The e-fold time of a mode (
), describes the time it takes for the signal amplitude to decay by a
factor 'e', i.e. the time it takes for the amplitude to decay from 1 to
.
The spatial modes are the eigenfunctions of the matrix and they are thus the empirically computed
eigenmodes of the system.
Note that B and G matrices are obtained solely from the time series data u(t). If the system is well
described by a linear Markov process, then our estimate of G will be independent of the choice of
. On the other hand, if nonlinear effects are important, then G will vary significantly with . As long
as the linear approach holds, the knowledge of the Green function can be used for short-time fore-
casting of the system behavior (ignoring the noise).
The matrix G is real, but non-symmetric, so eigenvalues
and corresponding eigen-vectors, -
functions and -modes are complex.
In theory the analysis could be applied directly on the state vectors of fluctuating velocity com-
ponents u(t), but even a modest sized vector map could quickly produce very large covariance
matrices, so computations would be come very CPU demanding.
PAGE|783
To mitigate this DynamicStudio applies the OPD analysis to the outcome of a previous Proper
Orthogonal Decomposition (POD Analysis), dramatically reducing the complexity of the analysis.
Stability analysis is performed on the Chronos of the POD modes and each eigenvalue provides dir-
ectly the frequency and e-fold time of a mode. Via the POD Topos corresponding eigenvectors are
mapped back to the spatial domain, producing complex spatial OPD modes.
Meaningful OPD analysis require time-resolved input. According to Nyquist theory we can resolve
frequencies up to half the sampling rate, meaning that the highest frequency is sampled twice per
cycle. In practice OPD analysis require more than 4 samples/cycle and we strongly recommend 6
samples/cycle. Reliable detection of low frequencies require the duration of the experiment
(sampling rate times number of samples) to cover a reasonable number of cycles. Again you
should aim for at least 4 cycles, preferably 6 or more.
The requirement of at least 4 complete cycles with at least 4 samples/cycle leads to a theoretical
minimum sample count of 16. In practice reliable results require a much higher number of samples,
at least 100 ideally 1000 or more.
Having selected an input ensemble of POD modes, the OPD Analysis is found in the analysis cat-
egory 'Vector & Derivatives':
The OPD recipe has two groups of settings, one to choose which POD modes to include or exclude
from the analysis, and another to sort and filter the resulting OPD modes:
PAGE|784
The first group 'Mode selection criteria' provides options to include or exclude various POD modes from the OPD analysis
All of these are optional and if none of them are selected the OPD-Analysis will include all but the
last of the POD modes:
The first two selection criteria are related to the Amplitude/Energy of the various POD modes:
l Setting a lower limit for Modal Energy Fraction will include all POD modes that contribute more
than the specified fraction of the total energy.
l Setting a lower limit for the Residual Energy will keep adding more POD modes until the resid-
ual energy is below the specified limit.
Please note that both Energy Fraction and Residual Energy are relative to the fluctuating energy,
i.e. excluding the dominant Mode 0, which is usually the DC and often contain orders of magnitude
more energy than all the other modes combined. Including this energy would make meaningful
recipe settings for these two parameters extremely small.
The last two selection criteria are related to the Chronos, one including POD modes, the other
potentially excluding them:
PAGE|785
l Temporally well resolved Chronos should correlate with themselves at small lags. The Lag-1
Auto-Correlation quantifies temporal coherence.
l The Kurtosis of a Chronos will be high for intermittent modes, where Chronos is almost zero
most of the time, but occasionally very large.
The first three of the criteria are 'Including' and a POD mode fulfilling any of them will be included.
The last of the four criteria is 'Excluding' and any POD mode with Kurtosis above the specified limit
will be excluded regardless of any other selection criteria.
To ensure that the OPD analysis can generate results, mode 0-2 is always included and the last of
the POD modes is always excluded, no matter which selection criteria are enabled and no matter
their limit values.
Typical level of Kurtosis-Values:
A Chronos with constant values will generate a Kurtosis-value of 1.0.
A Chronos describing a clean, noise-free sine-wave will generate a Kurtosis-value of 1.5.
A Chronos dominated by Gaussian white noise will theoretically generate Kurtosis-values around
3.0 (valid signal may be hiding in such noise).
Kurtosis-values significantly above this will typically come from Chronos with just a few large values
among a lot of very small ones. Such Chronos may be caused by and describe only undetected out-
liers in the input datasets and the corresponding modes should of course be excluded from a sub-
sequent analysis. If intermittent phenomena is present or expected in the experiment they too may
generate high Kurtosis-Values and should of course not be excluded, so in that case this test
should be disabled.
The group 'Post processing' contain various options to filter and sort OPD modes after they have been computed:
'Minimum accepted e-fold time / acquisition timestep' provides you with the option to discard modes
with exceptionally small e-fold times:
If the computed e-fold time is significantly smaller than the acquisition timestep you may question
the reliability of the result; How can you reasonably expect to say anything reliable about phe-
nomena that appear to have time scales significantly below the temporal resolution of your meas-
urement system? Indeed such modes rarely contain anything but noise and you may thus choose
to discard them altogether.
'Sort the OPD mode by ...'
Here you must choose to have the resulting OPD modes sorted by frequency (ascending), by e-fold
time (descending) or by periodicity (descending). If you wish to plot the results in a style similar to a
conventional frequency spectrum, sort by frequency. If on the other hand you want to see the most
interesting modes first, you should sort by e-fold time, since generally the longest e-fold times cor-
respond to the most interesting modes, showing the clearest coherent structures. Finally you may
choose to sort by 'Periodicity', which is the product of frequency and e-fold time. In this case the fist
modes listed will be the ones where e-fold time is long compared to the period of the corresponding
oscillation.
Output from the OPD Analysis
OPD Analysis generates modes, that are stored as separate datasets in an ensemble, but you can
not say beforehand how many there will be. The list of "raw" eigenvalues will of course contain as
many values as POD-modes included in the analysis, but the eigenvalues
typically come in
complex-conjugate pairs, where the one with negative imaginary part describes an oscillation with
negative frequency. Such modes with negative frequency are discarded since they provide essen-
tially the same information as their positive frequency counterparts. There may be several modes
with zero frequency, which are of course kept, so the number of OPD-modes will typically be some-
what larger than half the number of POD-modes included in the analysis. If you choose to discard
PAGE|786
modes with very small e-fold time the remaining number of OPD modes will of course be smaller
still.
As in POD Analysis Mode 0 will always be the temporal mean (DC) of the input datasets followed
by the actual OPD modes sorted as specified in the recipe.
The default display of an OPD mode is the spatial mode, inheriting the datatype of the ancestor
datasets; When the ancestor is a series of vector maps, all spatial modes will be vector maps also.
This is similar to the POD Topos, but where Topos are real the OPD modes are complex. If you
right-click the display of an OPD mode you can choose to 'Show Complex Vector Box':
The Complex Vector Box includes a slider, with which you can vary the phase angle used in the cur-
rent display; You can step forward or backward using PgUp/PgDn to change the Phase Angle in
steps of 15 degrees or you can move it back and forth manually with the mouse. You can also anim-
ate the phase angle forward or backward by clicking the play buttons. You can increase or reduce
animation speed by clicking repeatedly on the forward or backward buttons or stop it by clicking the
pause button. Provided the hardware supports it frame rate is fixed at 24 fps, while phase angle can
increase or decrease in steps of 1, 2, 3, 5, 9 or 15 degrees. The fastest option will animate a full
cycle in one second.
PAGE|787
Apart from the spatial distribution each mode has its own unique frequency and e-fold time, which
are accessible either numerically via 'Open as Numeric' or graphically via 'Open as XY Line Plot':
The first 4 columns contain Mode numbers and corresponding frequencies, e-fold times and peri-
odicity values. These are common for all modes and remain the same as you step through the
modes. Please note that Mode 0 (the mean) has been assigned an e-fold time of 0, even if the
mean by definition is assumed to remain constant over time and thus should have had an e-fold
time of infinity. Note also that the numerical display has two columns for each velocity component
so that you can see both real and imaginary part of the complex vectors.

16.67 Peak Validation
There are four possibilities to validate on the correlation peak.
Relative to zero peak is only used in Auto correlation
In Auto Correlation the zero peak represent the sum of all gray values in the images. The ideal
second highest peak is 0.5 height.
Relative to peak 2
This is the relative height of the highest peak compared to that of the second highest. In many
cases of few particles, this number is not very usable. For higher particle concentration, it is often
quite satisfactory to use 1.1. If a very strict validation is required a value as high as 2 can be used.
Peak width, Minimum & Maximum
The peak width is estimated with a 3 line parabolic fit in each direction and evaluated as the square
root of the product wx*wy (for more details see the reference manual). The peak widths are given in
pixels.
16.67.1 Interactive setting and finding good parameters
With an open vector map, it is possible to have the Validation box enabled (right-click on the map
and enable). It is at the same time possible to have an active histogram (right-click on the map and
choose histogram) of the peak widths. This gives the opportunity to find optimal settings in an inter-
active way.
Tool tip: On the vector map validation box, click on the slider and use the keyboard cursor for fine-
tuning.
16.67.2 Example using the peak validation for phase separation
The figure below shows an instantaneous snapshot of air bubbles injected into a water tank seeded
with red fluorescent particles. The top image comes from camera 1, which was fitted with a green fil-
ter. In principle, one should one see the bubbles. But as it can be seen on the histogram to the right
there is a large portion of correlation peaks around 2.3 pixels diameter. The reason being is that the
fluorescent particles also scatter some green light from their surface.
The bottom image comes from camera 2, which was fitted with a red filter. In principle only the seed-
ing should be seen. It is seen in the histogram, that the bubbles are seen as well. The scalar map in
between the picture and the histogram is the peak widths generated from 400 images using the
Average Correlation.
PAGE|793
Using the peak validation, based on judgement from the peak width proportions of the Average Cor-
relation, it was possible first to validate vector maps for identifying the fluid velocities represented
by the seeding with correlation peaks sizes around 2.3 pixels. The bobble velocities were found
using large interrogation regions and peak validation allowing only large correlation peaks.

16.68 Phase Boundary Detection
The phase boundary detection module takes an image or double-framed image dataset and
determines the phase boundaries in two-phase flows (flame fronts for combustion data or mixing of
two liquids, etc). The method uses a combination of global thresholding and local thresholding to
determine the phase boundaries. The gradient can also be used to subsequently filter away bound-
aries without a sharp gradient, which is mostly useful in flame front investigations in combustion dia-
gnostics.
There are three different forms of output depending on the user choice in the recipe:
l An image mask, where the output is 8-bit image where one phase has the pixel intensity 0 and
the other phase has the pixel intensity 255. This is normally used for Dynamic Masking of each
phase during phase separated PIV analysis.
l A boundary mask, where the output is 8-bit image where the pixels on the phase boundaries
have the pixel intensity 255 and the remaining pixels are 0. This line is normally used to visu-
alize the phase boundary. (red line in bottom right image in Fig. 1)
l A numeric dataset, where the output stores all the phase boundaries/flame fronts as a list of
pixel coordinates, as well as the phase tag and hierarchical information if available.
The GUI for the Phase Boundary Detection looks like this:
Fig. 1 Graphical user interface for the Phase Boundary Detection for a mixing experiment
16.68.1 A) Preview settings
Image number: The image index can be used to choose among the images from the parent
ensemble to be previewed.
Use region of interest: When checked, a ROI rectangle is added on the original (top left) preview
image, which can be used to define the ROI of the image. The other three preview images will only
show the chosen ROI. When dealing with combustion data, this should be used to define the ROI
such that the light sheet is placed on the boundary of the ROI. See Fig. 2.
PAGE|795
Preview mode: The preview mode drop down menu can be used to select to show the original,
threshold, gradient and result preview at the same time or show only a specific one of them in full
view.
16.68.2 B) Global threshold
Lower threshold: All pixels with intensity below this threshold are defined to be part of phase 2
(darker phase).
Upper threshold: All pixels with intensity above this threshold are defined to be part of phase 1
(brighter phase).
Suggest: When clicked, the module will attempt to find a suitable lower and upper global threshold
based on the currently selected preview image, which can still be further adjusted by the user.
16.68.3 C) Local threshold
Region size: The local threshold is computed for each pixel in the image to determine which phase
it belongs to. The local threshold is computed using Otsu's method on a region around the pixel.
The region size defines the width and height of this region, with origo at the pixel. For further inform-
ation on Otsu’s method: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otsu's_method. The phase 1 and 2 as a result
of the thresholding operations can be previewed in the “Thresholding” image (top right).
16.68.4 D) Filters
Flame filter: If checked, a gradient threshold is used to remove any found phase transitions without
a sharp gradient. This is especially useful for flame front investigations in combustion diagnostics,
where the flame front is by definition the surface where combustion is taking place, and not the
outer surface of the flame. See Fig. 2. Normally the flame filter is only used for detection of flame
fronts and is left unchecked otherwise.
Gradient threshold: The gradient threshold is one of the filters to remove unwanted sections of the
phase boundary computed as a result of the thresholding step. There is often sharp gradients on
the flame front, and smooth gradients at the outer edges of the flame where the flame diffuses
softly. The gradient threshold is adjusted to exclude the soft gradients which are not related to the
flame front.
PAGE|796
Fig. 2 Graphical user interface for the Phase Boundary Detection for a combustion diagnostics
experiment.
16.68.5 E) Output
Force closed contours: When flame filter is enabled, the method attempts to remove boundaries
without a sharp gradient. This will usually result in finding the boundary of the flame front as an
open contour of the actual flame front as shown in Fig. 3. With open contours, it is not possible to
produce a mask a mask of the different phases, so these output options are disabled. By enabling
“Force closed contours”, the method will attempt to keep contours closed such that phases can be
defined for each contour and masks can be outputted.
Mask of phase 1: The output dataset will be an 8-bit image mask, where all the pixels in phase 1
have the pixel intensity 255 and all the pixels in phase 2 have the pixel intensity 0.
Mask of phase 2: The output dataset will be an 8-bit image mask, where all the pixels in phase 2
have the pixel intensity 255 and all the pixels in phase 1 have the pixel intensity 0.
Boundary as image: The output dataset will be an 8-bit image mask, where all the pixels on the
phase boundary have the pixel intensity 255 and the remaining pixels are 0.
Boundary as numeric: The output dataset will be a numeric dataset, where all the phase bound-
aries are saved numerically as point lists.
Fig. 3 Graphical user interface for the Phase Boundary Detection for a combustion diagnostics
experiment with open contours.
16.68.6 F) Phase label
Phase 1: A custom name can be entered for phase 1, which will be saved in the numeric dataset.
Phase 2: A custom name can be entered for phase 2, which will be saved in the numeric dataset.

16.69 Dynamic Masking
The phase masks generated using Phase Boundary Detection can be used for dynamic masking.
Moving masks can be generated from the original image ensemble by isolating the moving object
that is to be masked. This can be achieved by using the image processing functions from Dynam-
icStudio's Image Processing Library or by using the Phase Boundary Detection. It is essential to get
zero gray scale values in the region that is to be masked out and non-zero gray scale values in the
rest of the image. Then the mask ensemble should be marked as such by checking the tick box
under “Custom Properties”. Like regular “static” image masks, the dynamic mask is defined as fixed
input by clicking on the space bar, and can then be applied on the particle images.
