18.10.7 Contours
As an third display option planar contour slices can be added to the display. The easiest way to add
contours slices is to use the probing feature. The probe is an interactive contour plane that can be
positioned (moved and resized) by using the mouse within the display window. When the probe is
in the correct position, it can be added as a contour slice, either by using the display options dialog
or directly from the context menu. The probe can optionally be restricted to move in a fixed plane, or
it can be moved freely. The probing feature is also available directly from the context menu of the
display window.
PAGE|1070
Left:Theprobeisdisplayedwithresizinghandlesineachcornerandarotationandtilthandleinthe
centeroftheplane.Right:Whenconvertingtheprobetoacontourslice,thehandlesareremoved.
Contour slices can also be added or updated manually by selecting a fixed plane perpendicular to
one of the 3 axes, or arbitrary by typing in the coordinates of 3 of the corners defining the plane in
the display options dialog. Like the other displays the color and the color map of the contour slices
can be changed to represent any scalar value available in the volumetric dataset. The color map
used by the probe will follow the color map for contours.
Any number of contour slices can be added to the display, and vectors, iso-surfaces and contour
slices can be displayed separately or combined for advanced displays. During investigation of your
data you may need to reset the camera using the context menu, to bring all data into the display.
PAGE|1071
18.10.8 Streamlines
The Streamline property tab is divided into four different parts. In the first you define the number of
seed points along the x-, y-, and z-axis, from these points the streamline integration starts. in the
integration type, it is defined if the streamlines are integrated in positive or negative vector direction
or in both directions. in the "Streamline colors" sections the color option is defined. here you can
select the variable to use for the color coding, also the color scheme and if needed a manual data
range can be selected. in the last tab, you can switch on or of "Arrows" as well as define their size
and amount along the streamline.
PAGE|1072
Exampleofasteamlinevisualizationoftheflowvelocityfromajetflow.
18.10.9 Legends
It is possible to add legends to a 3D view from any of the datasets shown in the 3D view.
A legend can be assigned to either, top, bottom, left or right.
If multiple datasets of the same type is shown in the 3D view, the name of the specific dataset is
appended to the name in the selection list.
The properties of the depicted legend (such as min, max values and color scheme of the legend)
are handled by the display layer for the specific dataset and can be changed by using the Display
Options dialog for a given layer.
PAGE|1073
18.10.10 Stereo Rendering
The 3D Display supports displaying the data in stereo rendering on the screen. There are 3 dif-
ferent modes supported:
l Red-Blue is supported for legacy use. This format can be used for displaying stereo on a stand-
ard monitor, but the effect is limited and the color spectrum is limited.
l Checkerboard requires active glasses synchronized to the monitor. Select this if your hardware
driver runs in checkerboard 3D mode.
l Shutterglasses requires active glasses synchronized to the monitor. Select this if your hard-
ware driver runs the shutterglasses mode. This mode gives the best effect and is fully color
neutral.
18.10.11 Animation
The 3D Display can be animated, automatically rotating the display to view the data from all sides.
This feature is especially informative when used together with the stereo rending feature.
18.10.12 Camera
Data can be viewed interactively using different camera modes:
l Trackball is a motion sensitive mode where motion occurs when the mouse button is pressed
while the mouse pointer is moved. This is the default mode.
l Joystick is a position sensitive mode where motion occurs continuously as long as the mouse
button is pressed.
l Flight is an animated mode where you interactively fly through you data.
Use Reset view to place your data in the center of the display window.
PAGE|1074
18.10.13 Export
The default export as image and display from the main menu of DynamicStudio is extended with a
local export option. This allows for more advanced export formats besides the standard bitmap
formats. The following formats are supported:
PNG
Portable Network Graphics (PNG) bitmap format. Provides lossless
data compression, popular for Web contents.
BMP
Bitmap Image File (BMP) bitmap format. Includes all pixels uncom-
pressed. This is probably the most compatible format, but generates
large files.
JPEG
JPEG (JPG, JPEG) bitmap format. Provides lossy compression gen-
erating very small images only suitable for e.g. E-mail and Web.
TIFF
Tagged Image File Format (TIF, TIFF) bitmap format. Used for scientific
imaging mainly.
EMF
Enhanced Meta File (EMF) vector and bitmap graphics format. Used
under Windows as the file containing calls directly to the GDI.
EPS
Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) text and vector graphics format. Widely
used and compatible with any dtp program.
VRML
Virtual Reality Modeling Language (VRML) 3D interactive vector graph-
ics format. This format is suitable for the Web and for backward com-
patibility.
X3D
X3D (X3D) 3D computer graphics XML-based file format. This format is
part of international ISO- and Open standards.
18.11 XY-Plot
The XY-Plot is used to show column based datasets using line, scatter or bar plot representation in
a 2D display
To open a XY-Plot of a dataset select the ensemble in the database and click 'Open XY-Plot' in the
'Home' Ribbon:
If XY-Plot is not an option for the selected data the 'Open XY-Plot' will be grayed out.
The default contents of a XY-Plot depends on the type of data plotted and/or the analysis method
creating the data.
Once a XY-Plot has been opened there are several options, all described below.
18.11.1 Graphical user interface
Right-clicking inside the XY-Plot opens a context menu like the one shown here:
PAGE|1075
The following possibilities are available from the context menu shown when right-clicking inside the
display:
l Display Options can also be accessed directly by double-clicking within the display window and
is described in details below.
l Analyze, Show Recipe and Perform Analysis Again refer to the data and not to the display,
which this help section is about.
l Reset Zoom will zoom out to either default or user defined range on all axes. The latter can be
set in “Display Options…” (see below)
l Show Legend can be toggled to show or hide a legend next to the plot. The legend is useful
when there are multiple curves in the same display.
l Probe is used to show numerical values close to where the mouse cursor is. It defaults to show-
ing values from the curve, but other options may be available depending on the type of data dis-
played.
l Show Grid can be toggled on or off to have a grid of dotted lines shown in the plot.
l Show Markers is a toggle option to show or hide markers defined by the dataset (can for
example be mean value). Not all data types have markers to show.
l
Info Box shows various dataset key information and statistics below the display and can be
toggled on or off.
l Copy to Clipboard will copy the current display to the Windows Clipboard to be pasted in else-
where.
18.11.2 Legend
When the legend is shown it is possible to highlight a curve in the display by clicking on it in the
legend. This can be useful if multiple curves are shown, to distinguish between them. To disable
highlighting click once more or right click on the legend and select “Deselect data”. The selected
dataset will be in red.
PAGE|1076
18.11.3 Info Box
The info box will show key information from the dataset. If this is of no interest or not available the
Info box can be switched off to make room for a larger plot.
18.11.4 Zooming
There are several ways of zooming in the XY-Plot. The mouse can be used, by pressing shift and
using the mouse to mark a rectangular area in the display, or by scrolling the mouse wheel. By
default the scroll wheel will zoom on all axes, but if Ctrl is pressed while scrolling it will zoom in/out
on the horizontal axis only and if Shift is pressed it will zoom on the vertical only. This kind of zoom
is temporary and can be undone by choosing 'Reset Zoom' in the context menu or simply by reopen-
ing the XY-Plot.. For a permanent zoom go to display options and specify user defined ranges on
all axes used. This zooming is permanent and will remain even when closing and reopening the
XY-Plot until the user actively switches back to 'Use full range' in the Display Options (see below)
The image below shows the rectangle being drawn when zooming with the mouse (the actual zoom-
ing takes place when the mouse button is released).
PAGE|1077
18.11.5 Probe
The Probe tool is used to show numerical values for data points in the plot. If one among several
curves have been selected in the legend the Probe tool will pick nearest point on the highlighted
curve, otherwise it will just snap to the nearest point on any of the curves. It defaults to showing
'Value', which is simply the x- and y-values of the data point chosen, but other values can be
chosen via the context menu. The values available to choose fro m depend on the dataset in ques-
tion, but can even be data not currently shown in the plot. For a histogram with percentage on the y-
axis the probe can for example be set to show the corresponding count or vice versa.
18.11.6 Default setup
For a newly created XY Plot the contents will depend on the data and the analysis method that cre-
ated it. It may look something like this, but it can always be modified in various ways:
PAGE|1078
18.11.7 Display Options
The display options have 4 tabs in order to simplify the user interface.
l Data selection
l Plot setup
l Axis setup
l Line style
Note, all settings can be applied without closing the display options dialog.
18.11.8 Data Selection
The data selection determines which curves are shown in the plot. Several sets of Y-values can be
chosen, but they must share one common set of X-values.
What exact values are available depends on the dataset in question, the figure below is just an
example:
Each of the curves can be set to display as 'Bar', 'Line' or 'Line2' by clicking the text in the right hand
side and choosing one in the resulting drop-down menu. 'Bar' means, that the corresponding data
will be displayed as a bar plot, while the default 'Line' means it will be shown as a curve. 'Line 2' is
also shown as a curve, but with a secondary y-axis that will appear in the right-hand side of the plot.
This can be useful when showing multiple curves with different value-ranges.
It is also possible to fit the data to a chosen distribution model and have the corresponding fit plot-
ted as well. To do so choose a distribution model in the bottom left of the Display setup and in the
bottom right choose which data to fit the model to. The resulting model fit will always be plotted with
a secondary y-axis in the right hand side of the XY-Plot.
Changes will take effect and the display be updated when 'OK' or 'Apply' is clicked.
PAGE|1079
18.11.9 Plot Setup
The plot setup is for setting general plot properties. A title can be written, some datasets supply
their own title, but can be overwritten if needed. The default title (if any) is available via the drop-
down arrow on the right.
The editable colors are axis color which include axis lines, numbers and labels. The title & legend
color applies to the title and the legend text. The plot back color applies to the background color of
the entire display. The legend back color applies to the background color of the legend area. Font
type applies to all text in the display except the info window. The currently selected type is shown
as an example beside the drop-down. The font sizes used in title, legend, probe text and axis labels
can be set individually.
18.11.10 Axis Setup
The axis setup provides the possibility to edit the axis labels the same way as the title. It is always
possible to get the default axis label from the drop-down.
PAGE|1080
It is possible to edit the range of values to be shown on all of the axes in the plot. If Full Range is
checked then all axis ranges will adapt to the data shown, otherwise the user must specify desired
minimum and maximum values for each of them.
All axes defaults to linear, but the user may switch to logarithmic for each of them by using the
check-boxes in the right hand side. For a logarithmic scale both min and max must be positive num-
bers.
When a secondary y-axis is used it can be forced to align with the primary y-axis by using the
check-box 'Map Y2- to Y-axis'.
All axes will by default be shown at the left, right or bottom of the display, but they can be forced to
go through zero on the other axis by 'Set axis origin to zero'.
Finally 'Transpose display' allows the user to plot the x-axis vertically and the y-axes horizontally if
so desired.
18.11.11 Line Style
The appearance of each curve can be changed with the following parameters:
l Line style
l Line color
l Line thickness
l Point symbol
l Symbol color
l Symbol size
PAGE|1081
Click either of these for any of the curves and a drop down will appear, where a different style,
color, thickness or size can be chosen. Line style can be set to 'No Line' to get a scatter plot show-
ing only data point markers. Similarly data markers can be set to 'No Symbol' to see curves only
with no markers. If both line and symbol style is set to none the corresponding curve will still be
there, but invisible.
18.12 Numeric Display
The Numeric display is a view of the raw data in the dataset. Unlike the more visual displays that
interpret the data in the dataset for visualization purposes, the numeric view shows the numeric val-
ues associated with the data points in the dataset. This could for example be the positions and
associated U, V and W values of a vector map. The numeric view shows the representation as the
data is exported if the dataset is exported as numeric values.
To see numerical values from a dataset select it in the database and then pick 'Open as Numeric'
from the Toolbar, in the Context Menu or in the File Menu:
PAGE|1082
The Numeric Display will show the numbers from a dataset in a spreadsheet style display with rows
and columns of cells, each with a number (or short text) in it. The exact content and layout of this
spreadsheet display will depend on the type of data shown. It is beyond the scope of this text to
describe them all, but a few examples and highlights will be shown here to show features that are
typical for the Numeric Display regardless of the data shown. Features that are specific for a spe-
cific datatype will normally be described in the Help page for the Analysis Method generating that
data.
The Numerical Display has a header explaining the content of each column.
For example Numeric Display of an image will by default look something like this (right half of the
figure below):
The leftmost (grey) column with the header # is simply a continuous number providing a unique ID
for each row. The next two columns with headers x & y are integer grid numbers, identifying each
vector's location as the x'th column and the y'th row. The next two columns are x & y again, but this
time floating point coordinates, describing the metric location of each pixel. In this example neigh-
bor pixels are 0.1mm apart. The grid indices for both x & y will always increase in steps of one, but
the metric positions may change if you move the origin or change the Scale Factor (See "Define
Axes" on page 105 for details about this).
The last column with the header 'Pixel' contain the actual grayscale values for each pixel. In the fig-
ure above some of the grayscale values have been highlighted in the Numeric Display and a
zoomed in Image Display, so you can see how the Numeric Display simply lists grayscale values
one row at a time starting in the bottom left corner of the image.
Specifically for images you can have the Numeric Display 'Show as Grid'; Right click somewhere in
the Numeric Display and pick 'Show as Grid' from the Context Menu:
PAGE|1083
Numeric Display changes to this view:
Rows and column of the numeric display in grid view match rows and columns of the image.
For vector maps the Numeric Display typically looks something like this (again showed side by side
with a zoomed in graphical display of the same data):
Each row corresponds to a specific vector and the Numeric Display lists vectors row by row starting
in the top left corner. In the figure above some of the vectors have been highlighted along with the
corresponding line in the Numeric Display to illustrate this row-by-row approach.
Again the leftmost (grey) column with the header # is simply a continuous number providing a
unique ID for each row in the table (i.e. each vector).
The next two columns are grid Indexes identifying vector location as the x'th column and the y'th
row in the vector map.
As implied by the names/headers x(pix) and y(pix) identify vector locations in pixel. Vectors are loc-
ated at the center of an Interrogation Area (IA), the size of which (Width & Height) is always an even
number of pixels. The center of the IA will thus always be at the corner of a pixel and not at the cen-
ter, which is why the vector pixel coordinates always ends on '.5'.
The next two columns x(mm) and y(mm) provide metric coordinates for each vector. These depend
on "Define Axes" on page 105 settings.
The remaining columns refer to the vector components;
PAGE|1084
Upix and Vpix specify the average particle image displacements in pixels as measured on the cam-
era sensor.
U and V are the same, but converted to metric velocities based on known scaling and time between
the two laser pulses that illuminated frame 1 & 2 respectively. Length is the Euclidian (metric)
length of the vector, i.e. the square root of the sum of squared vector components.
The Status Code is a binary coded integer with each bit having its own distinct meaning:
l 0: Vector is valid and derived from a specific peak in a correlation map
l 1: Vector is Rejected automatically (by software)
l 2: Vector is Rejected manually (by user; -legacy option)
l 4: Vector is Outside (by masking)
l 8: Vector is Disabled (by masking)
l 16: Vector is Substituted
The first and the last are considered valid vectors the others are not. Code 1 (Rejected by
software) is assigned by a validation routine if for example a vector differs too much from its nearest
neighbors. Code 2 (Rejected by user) is a legacy option from a time when the user could manually
click a specific vector and manually reject it. This is no longer supported and code 2 should never
be on. Status codes 4 & 8 can be assigned by applying a mask, where the definition of the mask
determine which of the codes to assign. 'Outside' is intended to deal with walls and objects in the
Field of View, while 'Disabled' is intended for areas such as shadows behind objects, where the
laser light does not reach and the flow present thus cannot be measured.
In practice it makes little difference if a vector is 'Outside' or 'Disabled', it is considered invalid in
both cases. In fact most analysis methods that check the Status Code care only if a vector is valid
or not and do not distinguish between different types of 'Invalid'. Code 16 is used to identify a vector
that is considered valid, but is not derived from a specific peak in a correlation map. Validation
routines that compare each vector to its neighbors can for example replace (/substitute) an invalid
vector with the average of its valid neighbors.
Status codes add up so a vector can for example have status code 17=1+16, meaning that it was
first rejected by a validation routine (1) and then replaced/substituted with a more likely vector (16).
Status codes can be inherited by derived data such as scalar map of e.g. Vorticity or they can be
assigned directly to various datasets by various Analysis Methods. They are used the same way
and mean the same in all contexts.
From the (right-click) context menu of a Numeric display you may choose to show the status codes
as text:
The result is that the numeric Status code is replaced by text such as this:
PAGE|1085
In case multiple codes are 'on' at the same time the one with the highest number is shown (which is
typically also the most important one).

Under the heading 'Decimals' in the right hand side there is an option to modify how floating point
values are shown in the Numeric Display. Default is 'Auto'. Clicking either of them shows a small
drop-down menu with possible alternatives:
'0 decimals' mean that the number will be rounded to the nearest integer and shown as such. The
options 1-6 decimals show the number with that exact number of decimals, 'Exponential' will switch
to exponential notation. 'Engineering' is also exponential notation, but with the 10-exponent always
a multiple of 3 and the mantissa fixed at 5 significant digits. The example below is the same dataset
with 'Length' set to 0, 2, 4, 6 decimals and then to 'Exponential' and 'Engineering' at the far right:

It is possible to sort the Numeric Display by the values in a specific column: This is done by double
clicking the header of the column to use as the sorting key. Double-clicking the column header
once more reverses the sorting order. Right-clicking inside the view and picking 'No sorting' in the
context menu returns the Numeric Display to the original row-order .

19 Dialogs
You can get help on dialog by pressing the F1 button.
19.1 Sort
Sorting enables you to change the sorting criterions for an ensemble. The sort option is available
through the context menu of an ensemble. The sort option will not be available if the selected
ensemble contains sub-ensembles or is analyzed.
By default all datasets in an ensemble are sorted after the acquired timestamp. Alternatively it is
possible to sort after a user selected dataset or by a user-defined property value. All sorting options
allows for descending sorting as well.
19.1.1 Sorting by Timestamp
By default sorting by timestamp is selected. The sort will look at the timestamps of all the included
datasets. Using this option is useful to restore the sorting if another sorting option has been applied
or to reorder the datasets if the ensemble was constructed by merge of two or more ensembles.
19.1.2 Sorting by Data Column Value
As an advanced option it is possible to sort the ensemble using an external dataset as Selection.
The only restrictions to the external dataset is that it must be generic curve data, and that the num-
ber of data points must match the number of datasets in the ensemble to sort. The external dataset
must be made as a user selection prior to using the sort option. In the sort option it is possible to
specify the generic column name to sort by.
This sorting option is very useful for sorting an ensemble based on analyzed data. As external data-
sets the Extract, Fit, and Profile analyzes are useful to define the sort order.
Example
This example shows how Analog Statistics and an Analog Transformation can be used as external
input to the Sort option. The Analog Transformation curve is selected as external user input to the
Sort. A duplicate is made of the original analog data, and the curve is used for sorting. As a result
the data corresponding to the smallest values are now listed on top of the sorted list.
PAGE|1089
19.1.3 Sort by Property Value
Sorting by a property value enables you to sort an ensemble based on property inputs. Custom
Properties can be dynamically added during saving data to the database or when using the acquis-
ition manager. The property type must be defined as a number value.
After sorting a special sort property is added to the record properties for the sorted ensemble. The
sort property contains the value used for the sorting, either from a timestamp, data column value, or
property value. The Split option uses this value to perform a custom split, and the value can be read
and used by analysis methods.
19.2 Split
Splitting enables you to split an ensemble into two or more ensembles. The split option is available
through the context menu of an ensemble. The split option will not be available if the selected
ensemble contains sub-ensembles or is analyzed.
The splitting will split the ensemble either on indexing or based on the current sort order. The cur-
rent ensemble will be included in the split as the first ensemble.
19.2.1 Split at Index
By default the ensemble is indexed starting at #1. Splitting at index defines a number of split widths
corresponding to number of datasets.
The table in the dialog will show where in the current ensemble the splitting will be performed.
Table contents:
"3: [1;4[ | 3" (meaning; the first split ensemble will hold 3 datasets. These datasets will be dataset
index 1, 2 and 3. Index 4 is not included in this ensemble)
"3: [4;7[ | 3" (meaning; the second split ensemble will hold 3 datasets. These datasets will dataset
be index 4, 5 and 6. Index 7 is not included in this ensemble)
"3: [7; 9]| 3" (meaning; the last split ensemble will hold 3 datasets. These datasets will be dataset
index 7, 8 and 9. Index 9 is included in this ensemble)
19.2.2 Split at Sort Property Value
The sort property value is added to the record properties of the ensemble, when an ensemble is sor-
ted using the sort option. Splitting at sort property value defines a number of split widths cor-
responding to the range of the sort property values.
The table in the dialog will show where in the current ensemble the splitting will be performed.
Table contents:
PAGE|1090
"1000: [200;1000[ | 4" (meaning; the first split ensemble will hold the first dataset up to sort value
1000. The datasets will be datasets that has the sort value 200 to 1000. Datasets that has the Sort
value 1000 and above in not included)
"1600: [1000;1600[| 3" (meaning; the second split ensemble will hold the first dataset up to sort
value 1600. The datasets will be datasets that has the sort value 1000 to 1600. Datasets that has
the Sort value 1600 and above in not included)
2000: [1600; 2000]| 2 (meaning; the last split ensemble will hold the first dataset up to sort value
2000 (highest sort value). The datasets will be datasets that has the sort value 1600 to 2000. )
19.2.3 Automatic
By default the split widths are calculated automatically defining a linear distribution of the widths
over the range. Using this option will ensure an equidistant and valid splitting.
19.2.4 Custom
Using the custom split widths, you can define your individual split widths in the list. In this case you
must ensure that the range is within the total range.
Select each of the width values in the list to set new values, press F2 to enter new split width value.
As a help defining the split widths the total range and the current range is automatically calculated
and displayed. If the current split is invalid, the conflicting position will be marked with a red color in
the list. Typically error situations are when too many splits are defined, or that some of the splits
become empty.
19.3 Merge
Merging enables you to combine results from two or more ensembles into one. The merge option is
available through the context menu of multiple selected ensembles. A number of limitations are
applied to merging ensembles; the data in the ensembles must be of similar type and size.
